propositions.text: The Appellant is a stateless Palestinian from Lebanon appealing the RPD's May 19, 2016 decision denying refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a stateless Palestinian whose country of habitual residence is Lebanon, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rendered on May 19, 2016, denying his claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Appellant is a stateless Palestinian from Lebanon appealing the RPD's May 19, 2016 refugee protection denial.

propositions.text: The Appellant does not request new evidence or a hearing before the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant does not request to submit new evidence in support of his appeal and does not request a hearing before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant does not request new evidence or a hearing before the RAD, as stated by the Appellant.

propositions.text: The Appellant requests the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find him a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA sections 96 or 97.
propositions.quote: The Appellant requests that the RAD set aside the determination of the RPD and find the Appellant to be a "Convention refugee" according to section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) or a "person in need of protection" according to section 97.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant requests the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find him a Convention refugee or person in need of protection under IRPA.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA s.111(1)(c), the RAD allows the appeal and refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a different panel.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to s. 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, the RAD allows the appeal and refers this matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal and refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a different panel under IRPA s.111(1)(c).

propositions.text: The Appellant was born in Lebanon to Palestinian parents, per his Basis of Claim.
propositions.quote: According to his Basic of Claim (BOC), the Appellant was born in Lebanon to Palestinian parents.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Appellant was born in Lebanon to Palestinian parents, per his Basis of Claim.

propositions.text: The Appellant moved as an infant to the UAE, was raised there, completed university, and had temporary resident status.
propositions.quote: As an infant, he moved to the United Arab Emirates (UAE) where he was raised by his parents and completed university in business. While in the UAE, the Appellant had temporary resident status.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Appellant moved as an infant to the UAE, was raised there, completed university, and had temporary resident status.

propositions.text: The Appellant and family are registered residents of a refugee camp in Lebanon and he visited grandparents there over the years.
propositions.quote: The Appellant and his family are officially registered as residents of the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp in XXXX, Lebanon. Over the years, the Appellant returned to Lebanon to visit his grandparents who reside in the camp.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Appellant and family are registered residents of a Lebanese refugee camp and he visited grandparents there.

propositions.text: In 2006, at age 16, the Appellant and twin brother were humiliated and shouted at by airport officials in Lebanon due to brother's name.
propositions.quote: In 2006, the Appellant (then aged 16 years) travelled with his twin brother to Lebanon. The Appellant's brother was interrogated at the airport given that he shares the same name as a known criminal in Lebanon. During this encounter, airport officials humiliated and shouted at the Appellant and his brother.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found that in 2006, the Appellant and brother were humiliated by Lebanese airport officials due to brother's name.

propositions.text: In 2010, the Appellant was interrogated and struck in the face by an officer in the refugee camp over alleged criminal connection.
propositions.quote: In 2010, the Appellant was visiting Lebanon when he was stopped by an officer who wanted to verify his identity upon entering the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp. The Appellant was interrogated by the officer who wanted to know if he was connected to a criminal named XXXX XXXX XXXX. The officer stuck the Appellant in the face and instructed him to remain in the camp until he returned to the UAE.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found that in 2010, the Appellant was interrogated and struck by an officer in the refugee camp over alleged criminal ties.

propositions.text: In 2014, the Appellant was stopped leaving the refugee camp, heard gunshots, injured his knee, and later had surgery in UAE.
propositions.quote: In 2014, the Appellant once again returned to Lebanon. While leaving the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp, he was stopped by an officer who checked his identity and instructed him to return to the camp. As the incident unfolded, gunshots could be heard inside the camp. In the ensuing commotion, the Appellant injured his knee. Unable to access proper care in Lebanon, he returned to the UAE where he eventually had surgery on his knee.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found that in 2014, the Appellant was stopped leaving the camp, heard gunshots, injured his knee, and had surgery in UAE.

propositions.text: In 2015, the Appellant lost his job and temporary residence permit in the UAE.
propositions.quote: In 2015, the Appellant lost his job as a XXXX XXXX in the UAE. This meant that he also lost his temporary residence permit which authorized him to re-enter the UAE.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found that in 2015, the Appellant lost his job and UAE temporary residence permit.

propositions.text: The Appellant fears returning to Lebanon due to violence in the refugee camp and family name association with targeted leader killed by terrorists.
propositions.quote: Following the loss of his job, the Appellant did not want to relocate to Lebanon where there are many gunfights in the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp to which the Lebanese authorities do not respond. In 2013, a XXXX leader named XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed by terrorists. The Appellant fears for his safety given that his family name is associated with this XXXX leader. People named "XXXX XXXX" are being targeted by terrorists and killed. The Appellant states that his relative named XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed in XXXX 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Appellant fears returning to Lebanon due to camp violence and family name linked to targeted leader killed by terrorists.

propositions.text: The Appellant alleges fear of persecution from cumulative racism and discrimination as a Palestinian in Lebanon.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Appellant alleges that he fears persecution based on the cumulative effect of racism and discrimination as a Palestinian in Lebanon where his basic human rights are not recognized.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant alleges fear of persecution from cumulative racism and discrimination as a Palestinian in Lebanon.

propositions.text: The Appellant arrived in the US on XXXX XXXX 2015 with a student visa and claimed refugee status in Canada on September 23, 2015.
propositions.quote: The Appellant arrived in the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2015 with a student visa. On XXXX XXXX, 2015 he came to Canada and made his refugee claim on September 23, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the Appellant arrived in the US with a student visa in 2015 and claimed refugee status in Canada on September 23, 2015.

propositions.text: The RPD recognized the Appellant is stateless Palestinian with Lebanon as habitual residence but rejected refugee claim due to credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RPD recognized that the Appellant is a stateless Palestinian and that Lebanon is the only country of habitual residence to which he can return. The RPD rejected the Appellant's refugee claim, concluding that he is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection based on overriding concerns related to his credibility.

propositions.text: The RPD found key aspects of the Appellant's evidence implausible, evasive, and identified unexplained discrepancies; documentary evidence did not overcome credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RPD found key aspects of the Appellant's evidence implausible and evasive and identified discrepancies which were not reasonably explained. Documentary evidence submitted to corroborate the claim could not overcome the overriding credibility concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant stateless Palestinian with Lebanon as habitual residence but rejected claim due to credibility concerns and implausible evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the Appellant does not face serious persecution or cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution in Lebanon.
propositions.quote: On the whole, the RPD concluded that "the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution in his country for being Palestinian or for any other reason, nor would there be a serious possibility of a cumulative effect of discrimination against him as a Palestinian amounting to persecution."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD concluded the Appellant does not face serious persecution or cumulative discrimination amounting to persecution in Lebanon.

propositions.text: The Appellant raises issues on appeal: RPD's credibility assessment, Internal Flight Alternative, and merits analysis errors.
propositions.quote: The Appellant raises the following issue on appeal: - Did the RPD err in the assessment of the Appellant's credibility? - Did the RPD err by finding that the Appellant can benefit from an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Lebanon? - Did the RPD err in the analysis of the merits of the claim?

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant raises issues on appeal about RPD's credibility, Internal Flight Alternative, and merits analysis errors.

propositions.text: IRPA sets grounds and remedies for appeal but does not specify RAD's standard of review for RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: The IRPA sets out grounds for appeal and possible remedies. However, it does not specify the standard by which the RAD is to review the decision of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA sets appeal grounds but does not specify RAD's standard of review for RPD decisions.

propositions.text: Huruglica holds RAD must analyze record to determine RPD errors and intervene if wrong in law, fact, or mixed fact and law when no credibility issue.
propositions.quote: In Huruglica,3 the Federal Court of Appeal held that after considering the RPD decision, the RAD is to carry out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. The role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in mixed fact and law, in cases which raise no issue with respect to the credibility of oral evidence.

propositions.text: RAD applies correctness standard when no credibility issue; for credibility findings, RAD uses case-by-case deference to RPD's oral evidence weight.
propositions.quote: In such cases, the RAD is to apply the correctness standard of review.4 With respect to findings based on credibility of oral testimony by the RPD, the court concluded that the RAD must take a case-by-case approach to the level of deference it owes to the relative weight of oral evidence tendered at the RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Huruglica holds RAD must analyze record for RPD errors, applying correctness standard if no credibility issue, and case-by-case deference for credibility findings.

propositions.text: A recent RAD panel held that when RPD has meaningful advantage on a finding, RAD may apply a reasonableness standard modified for RAD context.
propositions.quote: A recent three member panel RAD decision examined the standard of review applicable to credibility findings made by the RPD based on oral testimony. The RAD panel concluded that when the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, the RAD may assess that finding using a standard of reasonableness, modified to apply to the context of the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: A recent RAD panel held RAD may apply a reasonableness standard to RPD credibility findings when RPD has meaningful advantage.

propositions.text: Approach is to analyze record for RPD errors based on Memorandum of Appeal issues, then decide on evidence in record.
propositions.quote: my approach to the present appeal is to analyze the record and identify any errors that may have been committed by the RPD based on the issues identified in the Memorandum of Appeal

propositions.text: Will explain when deference to RPD credibility findings is warranted and how RPD had meaningful advantage.
propositions.quote: When deference is warranted, I will explain how the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage with respect to the finding in question.

paragraphs.summary: The court will analyze the record for RPD errors per the Memorandum of Appeal and explain when deference to RPD credibility findings is warranted.

propositions.text: Defer to RPD credibility findings but review refugee claim correctness standard.
propositions.quote: Although I may defer to findings made by the RPD with respect to the credibility of oral evidence, I will consider the RPD's determination of the refugee claim using a standard of correctness.

paragraphs.summary: The court will defer to RPD credibility findings but review the refugee claim correctness standard itself.

propositions.text: RPD erred in assessing Appellant's credibility, which is key to appeal.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD erred in the assessment of the Appellant's credibility which is determinative of the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD erred in assessing the Appellant's credibility, crucial to the appeal.

propositions.text: RPD found it implausible Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 after alleged mistreatment in 2006 and 2010.
propositions.quote: The RPD found it implausible that the Appellant would return to Lebanon in 2014 if he had actually been mistreated on previous trips in 2006 and 2010, as alleged.

propositions.text: RPD noted Appellant is well-educated and violence in refugee camps is well documented.
propositions.quote: The RPD considered that the Appellant is well-educated; violence in the refugee camps in Lebanon is well documented;

propositions.text: RPD noted people sharing Appellant's last name have been targeted by terrorists in the camp.
propositions.quote: the Appellant said that people who share his last name have been targeted by terrorists in the camp.

propositions.text: RPD rejected credibility of Appellant's mistreatment evidence during past trips.
propositions.quote: As such, the RPD rejected the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he was mistreated during past trips to Lebanon.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found it implausible the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 after alleged mistreatment and rejected his credibility on that evidence.

propositions.text: RPD's questioning was disparaging and unreasonably discounted Appellant's explanation for 2014 return.
propositions.quote: On appeal, it is submitted that the RPD's approach to questioning the Appellant was disparaging in nature. Moreover, the RPD unreasonably discounted the Appellant's explanation for returning to Lebanon in 2014.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits the RPD's questioning was disparaging and unreasonably discounted his explanation for returning in 2014.

propositions.text: RAD is equally placed to assess plausibility of this evidence aspect after reviewing record and hearing audio.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the entirety of the record and listened to the audio recording of the hearing, I consider that the RAD is equally placed to assess the plausibility of this aspect of the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RAD is equally placed to assess the plausibility of the evidence after reviewing the record and hearing audio.

propositions.text: RPD's inquisitorial process appropriately tests evidence plausibility by questioning Appellant.
propositions.quote: I begin my analysis by noting that the RPD hearing is an inquisitorial process which means that it is entirely appropriate for the RPD to test the evidence by asking questions about the plausibility of the Appellant's narrative.

propositions.text: RPD must test credibility of mistreatment evidence as central case issue.
propositions.quote: It was incumbent on the RPD to ask questions to test the credibility of the Appellant's evidence that he was mistreated during past visits to Lebanon as this was a central issue in the case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the RPD's inquisitorial questioning to test credibility of mistreatment evidence was appropriate and necessary.

propositions.text: RPD asked pointed questions and challenged Appellant but was not disparaging.
propositions.quote: My review of the audio recording reveals that the RPD asked the Appellant pointed questions and challenged him when he was not satisfied with a response. However, I cannot agree that the RPD was disparaging towards the Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD questioned the Appellant pointedly but was not disparaging.

propositions.text: RPD may consider plausibility, common sense, and reject evidence inconsistent with case probabilities.
propositions.quote: It is settled law that the RPD is entitled to consider plausibility, common sense and rationality when assessing a refugee claim. The RPD may reject evidence if it is not consistent with the probabilities affecting the case as a whole, even when that evidence is uncontradicted.

paragraphs.summary: It is settled law that the RPD may consider plausibility and reject evidence inconsistent with case probabilities.

propositions.text: Plausibility findings should be made only in clearest cases with reliable evidentiary base.
propositions.quote: This being said, plausibility findings should be made in only the clearest of cases. More specifically, the Federal Court cautions that the RPD should provide "a reliable and verifiable evidentiary base against which the plausibility of an applicant's evidence might be judged, otherwise a plausibility determination may be nothing more than "unfounded speculation."

paragraphs.summary: Federal Court cautions plausibility findings require reliable evidentiary base and only in clearest cases.

propositions.text: Is it plausible Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 despite alleged mistreatment in 2006 and 2010?
propositions.quote: Turning to the present case, is it plausible that the Appellant (a well-educated man) decided to return to Lebanon in 2014 if he was actually mistreated there in 2006 and 2010, as alleged?

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue whether it is plausible the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 despite alleged past mistreatment.

propositions.text: Appellant testified he was reluctant but pressured by mother to visit ailing grandparents in 2014.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified that he was reluctant to return to Lebanon in 2014 but that his mother pressured him to go "one last time" to spend time with his ailing grandparents who reside in the XXXX XXXX XXXX camp.

propositions.text: Appellant said his sole purpose in 2014 was to spend time with relatives, focusing on ailing grandparents.
propositions.quote: his sole purpose in returning to Lebanon in 2014 was to spend time with his relatives. When questioned about his actual activities during the 2014 trip, the Appellant maintained that his priority and focus was to spend time with his ailing grandparents.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appellant testified he was reluctant but pressured by mother to visit ailing grandparents in 2014.

propositions.text: 2014 trip purpose consistent with 2006 and 2010 trips focused on family visits at parents' behest.
propositions.quote: I note that the stated purpose of his 2014 trip is consistent with previous trips to Lebanon in 2006 and 2010 which occurred at the behest of his parents and were focused on spending time with his family.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the 2014 trip purpose aligns with prior family visits in 2006 and 2010.

propositions.text: Appellant's immediate family maintains close ties and financial support to relatives in the camp.
propositions.quote: The Appellant's immediate family maintains close ties with relatives who remain in the camp which lends weight to the plausibility of his decision to return to Lebanon in 2014. Indeed, the Appellant's father continues to provide financial support to his relatives who live in the camp.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appellant's family maintains close ties and financial support to relatives in the camp.

propositions.text: RPD erred by ignoring factual context supporting plausibility of 2014 return despite risks.
propositions.quote: As such, I consider that the RPD erred by reaching a plausibility finding by ignoring factual details providing important context to the Appellant's decision to return to Lebanon in 2014.

propositions.text: It is plausible Appellant returned in 2014 for final visit with grandparents despite risks.
propositions.quote: My analysis of the evidence leads to the conclusion that it is entirely plausible that the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 for a final visit with his grandparents notwithstanding any inherent risk attached to this endeavour.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD erred by ignoring context and concludes it is plausible the Appellant returned in 2014 despite risks.

propositions.text: RPD disbelieved Appellant's 2014 visit purpose due to discrepancy about 'vacation' wording.
propositions.quote: The RPD also did not believe that the Appellant returned to Lebanon in 2014 to visit his relatives based on a discrepancy in the evidence. In his BOC, the Appellant states that he returned to Lebanon in 2014 while "on vacation".

propositions.text: RPD remarked vacation means 'to have fun, to relax' and found it inconsistent with reluctant visit evidence.
propositions.quote: At the hearing, the RPD remarked that a vacation is "to have fun, to relax, that is my general idea of a vacation." The RPD found that being on "vacation" is different than the detailed evidence tendered by the Appellant at the hearing to the effect that he reluctantly went to Lebanon in 2014 when pressed by his mother to visit his sick grandparents one last time in the camp.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD disbelieved the Appellant's 2014 visit purpose due to a discrepancy about the meaning of 'vacation'.

propositions.text: Disagrees that 'vacation' means only fun or relaxing; it has broader plain meaning.
propositions.quote: With respect, I disagree that the word "vacation" is limited to "having fun or relaxing". The plain meaning of vacation denotes "a period spent away from home or business in travel or recreation; a scheduled period during which activity is suspended; a period of exemption from work granted to an employee; or a time of respite from something".

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees that 'vacation' means only fun or relaxing, noting its broader plain meaning.

propositions.text: Appellant's BOC use of 'vacation' means trip during work break, consistent with testimony.
propositions.quote: In the present case, the Appellant's BOC mentions that he returned to Lebanon in 2014 while on vacation. I take this to mean that he took a trip to Lebanon while on a break from his job in the UAE in 2014. This is largely consistent with the Appellant's testimony that he went to Lebanon during his annual holiday from his job in the UAE to visit his relatives in the camp.

propositions.text: Discrepancy identified by RPD is not real or rationally related to credibility assessment.
propositions.quote: In my view, the discrepancy identified by the RPD is not real and not rationally related to the assessment of the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the 'vacation' discrepancy is not real and consistent with testimony, thus irrelevant to credibility.

propositions.text: Appellant testified he will be in danger if returned because people sharing his last name were targeted by terrorists.
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified that he will be in danger if he returns to Lebanon because people who share his last name have been targeted by terrorists in the camp.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appellant testified he fears danger due to people sharing his last name being targeted.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant's evidence not credible as similarly situated relatives reported no problems with authorities or as Palestinians.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that the Appellant's evidence is not credible given that "similarly situated persons" such as the Appellant's twin brother, father and grandfather have not mentioned experiencing any problems with the authorities in Lebanon nor have they mentioned having problems as Palestinians in Lebanon as a result of being associated with the "XXXX XXXX" name.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Appellant's evidence not credible because similarly situated relatives reported no problems.

propositions.text: The RPD misapprehended the facts and erred in analyzing similarly situated persons.
propositions.quote: On appeal, it is argued that the RPD misapprehended the facts and erred in the analysis of similarly situated persons.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD misapprehended facts and erred analyzing similarly situated persons.

propositions.text: The RAD is equally placed to assess the Appellant's evidence on similarly situated persons, so RPD has no meaningful advantage on credibility here.
propositions.quote: I consider that the RAD is equally placed to assess the Appellant's evidence concerning "similarly situated persons" such that the RPD does not benefit from any meaningful advantage in assessing this aspect of the Appellant's credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD is equally placed to assess evidence on similarly situated persons; RPD has no meaningful advantage on credibility.

propositions.text: The RPD was correct to analyze similarly situated persons under s. 96 IRPA.
propositions.quote: I note at the outset that the RPD was correct to proceed with an analysis of "similarly situated persons" in the present case.

propositions.text: RPD may consider treatment of similarly situated individuals to establish persecution under s. 96 IRPA.
propositions.quote: the RPD is entitled to consider whether a claimant has established persecution under s. 96 of the IRPA through the treatment of similarly situated individuals to that of the refugee claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD was correct to analyze similarly situated persons under s. 96 IRPA, which allows such consideration.

propositions.text: Two key errors in RPD's assessment make the adverse credibility finding unsustainable: factual errors and failure to consider critical evidence.
propositions.quote: I have identified two key errors in the assessment conducted by the RPD which renders the adverse credibility finding unsustainable: first, the foundation of this finding is based on factual errors. Secondly, the RPD failed to consider critical evidence regarding similarly situated persons.

paragraphs.summary: Two key errors in RPD's assessment make adverse credibility finding unsustainable: factual errors and ignoring critical evidence.

propositions.text: RPD erred by wrongly stating the brother visited Lebanon 23 days; brother actually visited 2-3 days only.
propositions.quote: The Appellant did not say that his brother visited Lebanon for 23 days. He clearly testified that his brother spent "maybe 2 or 3 days only" visiting his grandparents when he returned to Lebanon in 2015.

propositions.text: RPD inaccurately found father and grandfather had no problems; Appellant testified grandfather is ill and he never asked about problems.
propositions.quote: the Appellant testified that his grandfather is an old man who is ill... he "never discusses with his grandfather if he suffered with anything" and he never asked his father and grandfather if they experienced problems in Lebanon.

paragraphs.summary: RPD erred on brother's visit length and inaccurately found no problems for father and grandfather; Appellant's testimony contradicts this.

propositions.text: RPD misapprehended evidence in concluding similarly situated persons did not experience problems in Lebanon.
propositions.quote: The RPD reached the conclusion that "similarly situated persons" such as the Appellant's twin brother, father and grandfather did not experience problems with the authorities in Lebanon nor did they experience problems as Palestinians in Lebanon based in part, on a misapprehension of the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: RPD misapprehended evidence concluding similarly situated persons did not experience problems in Lebanon.

propositions.text: RPD's factual errors led to disbelieving Appellant's danger claim and rejecting relevant news articles.
propositions.quote: It is plain to see that the factual errors made by the RPD had a far reaching impact on the overall decision to reject the credibility of this aspect of the claim.

paragraphs.summary: RPD's factual errors led to disbelieving Appellant's danger claim and rejecting relevant news articles.

propositions.text: RPD limited inquiry to brother, father, grandfather, ignoring other relevant evidence about a relative killed by terrorists in 2015.
propositions.quote: the RPD limited the inquiry of "similarly situated persons" to the Appellant's brother, father and grandfather... failed to consider other relevant information found in the Appellant's BOC stating that the Appellant's relative XXXX XXXX XXXX was killed by terrorists in the camp on XXXX XXXX, 2015.

paragraphs.summary: RPD limited inquiry to close relatives, ignoring other relevant evidence about a relative killed by terrorists in 2015.

propositions.text: RPD did not consider relevant BOC passage and never questioned Appellant on this issue at hearing.
propositions.quote: the RPD has not considered this information in the analysis. Moreover, my review of the audio recording reveals that this issue was never canvassed with the Appellant at the hearing.

paragraphs.summary: RPD did not consider relevant BOC evidence and never questioned Appellant on it at hearing.

propositions.text: RPD's finding that Appellant faces no danger from name-based targeting is unsustainable due to failure to consider all evidence.
propositions.quote: This finding is unsustainable given that the RPD failed to consider all the Appellant's available evidence concerning "similarly situated individuals."

paragraphs.summary: RPD's finding that Appellant faces no danger from name-based targeting is unsustainable due to ignoring evidence.

propositions.text: RPD asked if Appellant could rent outside camp; Appellant said no due to finances and discrimination.
propositions.quote: the RPD asked the Appellant if he could rent an apartment outside the camp upon his return to Lebanon. The Appellant explained that it would be difficult for him to get an apartment outside the camp because he does not have the financial means to do so and he would be unable to find a job in Lebanon where he faces discrimination as a Palestinian.

propositions.text: Appellant conceded father would help financially if needed despite financial difficulties.
propositions.quote: the Appellant conceded that his father would undoubtedly come to his aid if he found himself in a dire situation requiring financial assistance upon his return to Lebanon.

paragraphs.summary: RPD asked about renting outside camp; Appellant said difficult due to finances and discrimination but father would help if needed.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant evasive about family's wealth and father's ability to support, undermining credibility on internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Appellant's evidence to be evasive with respect to his family's wealth and his father's ability to support him. The RPD concluded that this aspect of the "Appellant's evidence is unsatisfactory and undermines his credibility regarding his financial means to live outside the refugee camp as an internal flight alternative (IFA)."

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Appellant evasive about family's wealth and father's support, undermining credibility on internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: RPD may reach negative credibility finding if claimant's evidence is vague, indicating evasiveness.
propositions.quote: the RPD is entitled to reach a negative credibility finding when the claimant's evidence is couched in vague terms. After all, this type of evidence may be a strong indicator that a witness is attempting to be evasive.

paragraphs.summary: RPD may find negative credibility if claimant's evidence is vague, indicating evasiveness.

propositions.text: Deference is owed to RPD's credibility findings based on oral testimony and witness observation; reasonableness standard applies.
propositions.quote: As such deference is owed to the RPD which means that I will assess this finding on a reasonableness standard.

paragraphs.summary: Deference is owed to RPD's credibility findings; reasonableness standard applies.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony was forthright about father's financial support; no evidence of evasiveness undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the record and audio recording of the RPD which reveals that the Appellant's testimony was forthright about the fact that his father guaranteed an amount of $200,000 as security so that he could obtain his student visa to the USA.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant's testimony was forthright about father's financial support; no evasiveness undermining credibility.

propositions.text: RPD speculated without evidence that father would support Appellant indefinitely; this is flawed and ignores Appellant's individual claim.
propositions.quote: I must agree with Appellant's counsel who submits that the RPD engaged in speculation when reaching the conclusion that the Appellant should be able to count on his father's generosity to support him for an indefinite period of time in Lebanon.

paragraphs.summary: RPD speculated without evidence that father would support Appellant indefinitely; this is flawed and ignores individual claim.

propositions.text: RPD accepted some documentary evidence showing Appellant's official refugee camp residence and Lebanon as country of habitual residence.
propositions.quote: the RPD gave probative weight to documents produced after the hearing recognizing that the Appellant is officially registered as residing at the XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee camp and that Lebanon is the only country of habitual residence where the Appellant, as a stateless Palestinian, can return.

paragraphs.summary: RPD accepted some documentary evidence showing Appellant's refugee camp residence and Lebanon as habitual residence.

propositions.text: RPD rejected documentary evidence about Palestinians' treatment in Lebanon as not probative, similar to NDP information.
propositions.quote: no probative weight was given to documentary information submitted by the Appellant about the treatment of Palestinians in Lebanon.

propositions.text: RPD found claimant's lack of credibility and objective evidence do not show serious persecution or cumulative discrimination.
propositions.quote: The claimant's probative evidence regarding his personal circumstances as a Palestinian in Lebanon, considered with his lack of credibility regarding past mistreatment in Lebanon and considered with the objective evidence regarding the treatment of Palestinians generally in Lebanon, does not show that the claimant would face a serious possibility of persecution or the cumulative effect of discrimination amounting to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: RPD rejected documentary evidence on Palestinians' treatment as not probative, finding no serious persecution or cumulative discrimination.

propositions.text: RPD's conclusion rejecting documentary evidence is arbitrary and not founded on evidence.
propositions.quote: On appeal it is submitted that the conclusion reached by the RPD is arbitrary and not founded on the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant submits RPD's conclusion rejecting documentary evidence is arbitrary and unfounded.

propositions.text: RPD failed to explain why documentary evidence on Palestinians' conditions does not amount to persecution despite acknowledging restrictions.
propositions.quote: the RPD failed to articulate any reasons to explain why the documentary evidence concerning the conditions of Palestinians living in Lebanon does not amount to persecution.

paragraphs.summary: RPD failed to explain why documentary evidence on Palestinians' conditions does not amount to persecution despite acknowledging restrictions.

propositions.text: The RPD erred because its finding lacks any analysis or explanation.
propositions.quote: the RPD erred because this finding is not supported by any analysis or explanation.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD erred due to lack of analysis or explanation for its finding.

propositions.text: I independently analyzed the record, listened to the audio, considered the Appellant's arguments, and reviewed the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: I have independently analyzed the record, listened to the audio recording, considered the Appellants' arguments and reviewed the RPD decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states it independently analyzed the record, audio, arguments, and RPD decision.

propositions.text: The RPD identified credibility as the central issue.
propositions.quote: the RPD identified credibility as the central issue.

propositions.text: The RPD could make adverse credibility findings based on evasive, implausible, and contradictory testimony.
propositions.quote: it was open for the RPD to make adverse credibility findings based on testimony that was evasive, implausible and contradictory

propositions.text: The court found several errors in the RPD's findings that are unsustainable and determinative of the appeal.
propositions.quote: my review of the evidence has led me to identify several errors in the RPD's findings which are unsustainable and determinative of the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds credibility was central, adverse findings were permissible, but identifies unsustainable errors in RPD's findings.

propositions.text: The court cannot confirm or substitute the RPD decision without hearing the Appellant's oral testimony and weighing evidence on credibility.
propositions.quote: I am unable to confirm or substitute the RPD decision without hearing the Appellant's oral testimony and weighing evidence presented by the Appellant with respect to his credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court cannot confirm or substitute the RPD decision without hearing the Appellant's oral testimony on credibility.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA ss. 111(1)(c), the matter is referred back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: Therefore, pursuant to ss. 111(1)(c) of the IRPA, I refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court refers the matter back to the RPD for re-determination by a different panel under IRPA ss. 111(1)(c).

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed.
propositions.quote: The appeal is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal.
